HINTS ON Canner Parrenns.—Carpet patterns may with I advantage have a gmmetrical formation, for this gives to the mind an idea of order or arrangnment When the pattern has not a geometrical basis a general evenness of ...trines should be preserved. At once self- ! constituted judges and executionms, the abbess and her ! reverend coadjutors proceeded forthwith to enforce their 1 barbarous sentence in the following manner. Having con- veyed their victim to a esti in which an iron stove stool out from he wall, they causal the stove to be heated in her presence, and then. tying her hands tightly together behind . her hank, held her face down tor several num., close to ! the surface of the glowing metal. LORD ILLICIINOToN.—Lord Hartington haa had bite chance. It is no eXaggeration to say that he had made for hirneelf a position which is hoodiit uulq,ie. A melodious and finished elOcutionist he cannot be called. But the matter of hie remarks, and, independently of his voice, their manner, are of the Itiglie.t excellence. He has convinced the House of Cumulous, a whole, that, while he has every consideration for it, he is not in the slighest degree afraid of it. He has done what few Whigs have ever dine—he has won the con- fidence of the Radicals without wrangle, the Wlngs them- selves. Lord Harrington knows that, in the state of things under which we are now living, eerions changes are destined to take place. Heir prepared, not to accelerate, hut not to resist, the inevitable. The poi etician who would precipitate change is a revolutionist the politician who, convinced that certain chmges are dictated by a law as inevitable aa that of gravitation, is willing to be instrumental in these changes, may be called a Radical, but is really an enlightened states- man. L.," I limy state that in regard fie the origin el the practice of eating geese, the popular tradition is that Queen Elizabeth on her way to Tilbury Fort, on the 29th September, 1588, dined at the ancient seat .181 c Neville Untheyville, where, among other things two BM gone were priaided for thinner The Queen, having Gable heartily, called for a bumper of Burgundy, and gave as a toast ° Beetruction to the Spanish Arniad..." a• A. will be iMerested to learn that the "calumet " is a symbolical instrument of great importance among the , American Indians. It in api pe, whose bowl is generally I naadeataeottetdntorblei the tube of a very long reed,' ornamented with wings anti feathers of birds. No affair of consequence is transacted with the calumet. It appears in meetings of commerce or exchanges, and in congresses ; for determining peace or war. The acceptance of the calumet is a mark Di concurrence with the terme proposed, es a , rofusal is a certain mark of rejection. Even in the rage of a conflict this pine in sometimes offered ; and if accepted, the weapons of deetructinta instantly drop from Choir hands, and a truce enrolee The rnlumet of peter in different from that of war. They make urn of the former to seal their , alliances and treaties, to travel with safety and to receive , otrangere; but of the latter to proclaim war. It consists of a red stone, like marble, formed into a cavity resembling the , head of a tobacco pipe, end fixed to a hollow reed. They adorn it with teathere of various colours, rend name it the , calumet of the sun, to which luminary they present it, in expectation of thereby obtaining a change of weather as I , often as they desire. From the winged ornaments of the , “lumet, an.l its conciliating use, writers compare it to the I caduceue of Mercury, which was carried by the caduceatore of peace, with terms to the hostile tribes. The dance of the calumet is c. srlemn rite among the Indians on various I occasions. They dare not wash themselves in rivers in the beginning of summer, nor taste of the new fruit., without performing it; and the same ceremony alwaye confirms , a peace or precedes • war. It is performed in , winter in their cabins, and in narrower in the open fields. I For this purpose they choose a spot among trees to shade , thein from the heat of the sun, and lay in the middle A large ; mat as a carpet. setting upon it the god of the chief of the I conapany. On the right hand of this image they place the ; calumet, cc their great deity, erecting around ten kind of ' trophy with their arms. The hour of dancing being come, I those who are to sing take the most honourable seats under the shads of the trees. The company is then ranged round, , everyone, before he site draw, saluting the monitor, which is , done by blowing upon it the smoke of their tobacco. Each person next receives the calumet in rotation, and holding it with both hands, dances to tlie calence of the vocal music, which is accompanied with the beating of a sort of drum. I During this exercise it, gives a nignel to one of the warriors, who lakes a ban, arrow. and axe. from the trophies already mentioned, and tights lrirrti the former alehntling himself with the calumet only, anti bah of been dancing all the while. DIN mock engagement being ov r he who holds ' the cal owl make, a wed, in which he gives an amount of the battles he free fought and the prisoners he has taken, and then receives a cloak or some ether present from the chief of the ball. He then resigns the GAIUITITT to Another, who, having acted a similar part. delivers it tn a third, anti heloa fourth, he., till at last the instrument returns to floe per,on s Ito began the ceremony, and who presents it to the nation invited to the feast an a mark of their friend- ship and a confirmation of their alliance. div.p: WINSFORD.

COMPRIMTION FOR LARD ,•CEASIORMCS.—The followitm petition. going the round of Winsfrod this week the chairman and member. of tie Winsford Local Board. The petition of the undersigned property owners and rate. payers within the Local Board district of Wineford showeth I, That great damage is done to property in this district by the subsidence of lan4, noosed by the abstraction of brine. 2. That your petitioners are of opinion that compensation should be paid for such damage, especially when it is bump its mind that the rock salt which is abstracted in the shapo of brine from under the dam:us:al premise, is the sole and exclusive property of the person whoee premises are being damaged. 3. Your petitionere would also remind the Board that tithe rock salt was mined in the ordinary wav, a royalty or Touchene would be paid, but because it is token away in brine no royalty in paid and the owner,' property damaged in addition. This seems to an unfair and unjust; and in the aimed correajmnding can of collieries full conipenation would have to be paid for all property damaged. 4, That your petitioners are of opinion that there ire very serious waste of bt and that millions of gallons might he saved by proper prectutiens. This alone, if regulated, would form every large compensation fund. Thin waste seems to us positively inignitous, especially when the great dentruc- lion of property in the district is taken into consideration. 5, That the payment of compensation would not, in our opinion, affect the salt trade in the leant. This is condo- sively shown by the fact tier the price of salt has vane,. j more than line shillings per LAW, not the cost of freight to America ban also varied as much ten and fifteen shilling@ per ton, yet the demand from that country is greater than ever it was. 0, That we respectfuily submit that this If It question in which the Boned shoold 1a.., some action con- jointly with the Nmthwich Loc d 800- ' and the property owner, of the two district.; that the rates are heavier in consequence of the increased cost of laying arel maintaining sower, ofrulne, w.iter and gas pipes, and also by the assets,- mentos being reduced for damaged and destroyed property. 7, That although mote parts of the district may not be effected at the present time, the vast quantity of brine pumped up (estimated at eleven hundred minim gallons, without considering waste) must certainly affect large areas of other property at no distant time. Your petitioners there- fore humbly pray that the Board will be plea.ed to act con- jointly with the Northwich Local Board and floe property owners in the promotion of a private bill in Part iainent to obtain mach remedienand redress for the matters complained of an may be considered bent. And your petitioners will Tw ever pray, kc. (130VRICIOIRNi SCIE,CI3 SCIIOOI, WINSFORD.—The head master (Mr. John Buckley) of the Government Science Chimes, held at the Academy. Wthsford, has been rewarded daring the week by additional certificate. as the result of the winter's labours and the June and July exertions at South Kensington Institution, Igmtlon. In light he is placed let off. division, and in magnstism!ind electricity sth of I. ditheion. Ile has also trained lits biology and applied mechanin certificates, en that he now possesses MS first, fourteen second, and two third-cla. certificate. from London examining bodies on education, acience, art, and muck The same appli. to Mr. 11. Vivian Buckley, the second master. The facilities offered by Government for the de- velopment of science and its extension among all claws, have been laid hold of at Wineford. In additton to the ecientific knowledge acquired by the master, this school has oleo considerably enlarged the stock of ecientific apparatus for teaching the eciences in the experimental manner, so suc- cessfully pursued at the School of Phynics at Smith Ken. sington. The continuous encrturagem. at of high-teaching or extension of elementary education in the direction of science has done much to perfect that which was lacking in the educational scheme for Great Britain and Ireland. Through it anay young man who has received a fair ele- menMry statue may continue his education instead of let- ting drop all the good affected, at no inconaiderable outlay, either directly fto:n Government or local t.,gation, in addi- tion to what hi. parents may havedene. It is owing to the fostering care that ma artiz ins ore rising in estimrtion as workmen. This was the result anticipated by the late Prince Consort, and will ardently be desired by every well-wisher of his country. Thougli much has been done, much re- main to follow ; this especially applies to Winsfard. where every effort of the committee in ably supported by the mienoo master, who are beginning to enrol students for the recommencement of the winter campaign, as announced M , our advertising columns.. •

AUX°. Fence AT ALTHINCWAY.— Samuel Robinson Chic was charged at the Altrinch im Police Court, on Satur- day, whir obtaining by false pretences 15s. from Mr. W. H. vetei inary surgeon, Altrincham. and 15s. front Mr. Joseph Harris, clerk to the Al trincham Bench of Magistrates. On the 1411, inst the prisoner went to Mr. Pugh's place, represented that he had been sent by Mr. Mercer, auctionees, of Manchester—in whose einploy he fornierly was—for 15e., and he gave off 111, which purported tube in the hen& writing of Mr. Mercer, for the money. The prisoner repre- sented that ss. were required to pry wine taxes in a case of distraint and tos. to pay for muting some bills of the sale. Mr. Mercer elated that the primner was in his employ IS months ago, but had nit been eince. The letter WAA not in his handwriting, and he gave him no authority to borrow the money. Mr. Harris fatted that on the previous day the prisoner cane' to his office with a letter stating that Mr. Mercer hail taken possession of a house at reel Causeway under a bill of sale for .£llO, and that he was short of 15s. Ito pay the rent. The prisoner stated tha- the house WAS Mr. Marriott's or Mr. Murray's. He asked the prisoner whether he was still a clerk in the employ of Mr. Mercer, and he I stated that lie was. He advanc.ed the money, and the prisoner gave a receipt signsd "J. Wood." Mr. 'Mercer also denied that in this case he gore she prisoner any authority to use his name or to borrow the money, and add it was not true that he was in possession of a house at Peel Causeway. The prisoner was committed for trial. Annoy AT THE DUNNAINI MASSIre STATION.--74, Ed- want Lawson, auctioneer, Manch, stir. was charged at the Sale Petty Sessions, on Monday, with assaulting Joseph Cantrell, the stationmaster at Itunliem Massey Station, on the 21st inst. The defendant went to the station write time after the list train had guest, Manchester and asked the complainant how he war to get to Manchester. He had a ticket from Thelwall to Sale, and had broken the jonmey at Dunham by the consent of the official who was collecting the ticket.. The Complainant took the ticket from the de- fendant, and refused to give him the value of it. They had an altercation, and the complainant ordered the defendant away. He was proceeding to remove front the station witen the defendant struck him.—The defendant stated that lie in- quired whether he could get to Nlanchester hy Warrington, and asked for an esplanation with regurd to his ticket, whereupon the complainant till him to get off the station; he also Raid hewould not hook him to Warrington. The complainant fetched a lamp. and in attempting to strike him on the head with ir he stmok hien on the arm, broke the

He was treated at the railway At than in a most scand.dons man- ner. and he W. astonished when he heard the chvgc made against him.—The Bench dismissed the case.

WHERE SHALT, WE GO FOR OUR HOLIDAYS? Sir —This all important and ever recurring question is Ca the fore agai. This is the time when the various merits and disadvantages of the local watering places are weighed and conaidered. Now, eir, it seems to be a toti,ng with burnahity to feel itself impelled to go for a-field for what can be obtained quite as good and much cheaper at their awn doors We, to Warrington, living on the very highway to some of the niceet watering places in the oeighbourLood, rock off by steam to Blackpool, Isle of Man, Llandudno, or some other overerowthal sea-side resort. lain astonished at the 'ententeor noble river receives. a memo of pleasant recrea- tion. 1 an, sure Or scenery will compere vervfavotrably with that of Blackpool or Southport, except, indeed, that Eind actuary the old man admired so much at the latter pit viz., the muds and the swing., to my nothing of the Riga end christv minstrels! Barring these and kindred jam (> all the real °teapotr, and advantagee of a sea-side sojourn Gan be obtained on the river and M the hey with leer annoyance and eta tithe of the met. Here is the Aldine of O trip I had this week in a fifteen feet open boat. Shipping en captain, crew, cook, and cabin hop, with all negrausty Canto and msterials appertaining to these seve-al not forgetting Oat inord important adjunct the black.backed banjo, which, over alp at fire when well tilled, makeo music well calculated to moth the savage breast of a lologrY moo, we, that is to say the pair of on, the Doctor and I. started about noon from the bridge, intending to get as for duwn as pomible before the tide. This occurred at the bottom of Bank Quay reach, where the necessary stoppage was taken zsdrantage of to dine,ao interludewithout the accompaniment of the above-nientioned musical instrument, not having time fora full display. The incoming tide havir r slackened a little we stole aMng the stiller parts of the current before a light but favoureble niod, and reached Fidler's Ferry before high water. The rapid ebb and following wind carried no quickly by Runcorn, Weston, Hale Head, and Oglet Point, where near the lightship I ordered the crew to furl the sails anti unghip the ~,or or the wind had left us entirely at the mercy of Occurrent. They all obeyed witti alacrity, and took to the 011 re and pulled with ,will. In sneerer to a hail from the lightship as to "where we two" were goiag, and if we were for "bobbing," I disclaimed any inclination towarda eel murder, and announced New Brighton as our deetination. I was informed that the eels were doing nothing, that is doing the best for thenmelvec end keeping Ott of the way of temptation, and ultimately, the banjo, where they dance to music of their own making. Swiftly past Garston the rapid current carried to triumphantly sea- ward, past fishermen bury emptying and washing their nets, pant vessels at encl., with straining cables and boiling bows, onward towards the setting son swiftly on the 'wiling eddies, borne upon these rising waters eager for the sea The shallow rapids of the Dingle quickly emptied ue into the deeper waters of the Sloyne, where may be seen in close proximity the old 0 wooden walls "of old England and the modern iroulad. Here a welcome breeze made itself felt, and piping all hands to make mu it carried um swiftly through the tutnbling turbulance of the Liverpool channel. Through the deepening gloom, past iron monsters straining at their cables as though eager for the sea, part crowded New Brigh!on boats which rapidly emerging from out the gloom ahead, are quickly lost in the obswrity astern, on, I and the Doctor tumbling upon the mething watere they have left, past New Brighton stage and pier, gay with lights and music, below and in shore of which, I Inman the pier and not the music, we let go anchor and made things stingier the night. And now odol-eyed monsters came out of the darkness and made toot to the stage, and took into Rs capacious maw hundreds of people, and 11111111 gt the ringing of bells and the ecreaming of steam atole again into the darkness. Finally the band played "God rave the Queen." By the way Ed , Mi. itor, I believe the next generation are to have a new anthem—"Ool save the country." The last boat left with its human freight, the last of the stragglers left the beech, and the Doctor and I were left alone upon the waters to eleep rocked upon the ever heaving waters, with the weal] of the eurt for a lullaby, end beneath the vigilant anti revolving eye of the rock light. So paean the night, which wee warm and calm—en much . so indeed that the awning never was rigged being slept upon instead of under, until hell-past one, when all hands were piped to make sail and weigh anchor. On awakening at this time the tide was found to be running out in shore, although not high eater, and certain dark objects would be ditnly discerned by the aid of high but feeble moon drifting out to sea, evidently bound down the Rock Channel, gs were we. They were soon lost to sight in the miety atmosphere, hut we stole after them beneath the symmetrical shaft td the rock light keeping well in shore for the better title anti fore better reason still: that little fur- ther out and we were 000 01 sight of land, and being with- out compass or chart had nothing to steer by tire the incon- stant moon. Indeed, it our track could be accurately Laid down I am afield it would have a very dog-legged look and be found to have a many We in it. When one boric be simultaneously oarsman, helmsman, and lookout some little deviation from the proper course icon be expected. Before losing might of the rook light right astern I had the moon in the weather (port) quarter, and kept her there (more or less) until making Lemur. light. Here! come up with the yeapele which passed me at New Brighton, gliding on the airlese sea in ghogt-like stillness. We now laid the hoat's head inehoreand crossed the Dove Spit; here we met the fishing fleet coming out of the lake. Mutnal matutinal mlutations having passed, we were informed that the course we were then eteering would bring us into the lake, which it did. And then the day broke, we let go the anchor, the cook made es some coftee, and the hands were piped down. When we awoke we found tunnel ves—not on a hetl of roses brit a lied

of mussels, of which fact we proceeded to take advantage and plucked some of the feathers from that bed. Mussels are very "clannish" things—beat al. the mee hollow for this, to gathering theft you do not collect them indiscri- s minately, but cilef tiny select the heads of the family, leaving those of Roder years for growth and improvement, ' taking in preference their uncles and aunts, not neglecting even the oldest patriarch of the bunch with shell encusted o'er with parasitic relatives and large enough to be the feed- ing ground of the perriwinkle. Now the tide came and with it the necessity for action. Now, actions in war are, I believe, generally preceded by music in some form or other. Determined to follow en lendable example, I pro- duced from its dark retreat in the locker, the "banjo," and forthwith pl yed a se° thereon. A eliced onion, some tin beef—opened by the jack knife and coal hammer—a little pepper, salt, and butter, and an appetite worthy of the cause. We hod just closed thisconcert of one when the Doctor was holiest by a resident acquaintance who IT9B boxing about in his yacht, and asked if we were not ready for a crulee. Of course we were! After ouch s dinner ready for anything! So the hands were piped away to make sail and weigh, and we Mood after our friend towards Leasowe Lighthouse, and then bore up again for the lake and through it to Hilbre Island. The •ight of its wave-worn rocks reminded on very ! forcibly of our last visit in .other ship some three weeks before. We had just come up the wash and anchored under ' the island and svere replenishing the inner man, when we heart shoute astern and caw people waving their handker- chiefs on the rock between the two islands. On going to them they pthved to bra family party from Liverpool, who ' came over the sands in a trap and had been cthght by the Ode. They were all more or less wet, emus of the ladies having been wading waist-deep, which naturally made them anxious to gam drier quarters. 8o we took our angelic cargo shooed, ainirlst much fun and merriment, the ladies making light of their troubles, and transferred them to the larger island, in a saudy cove of which they proceeded at once to make things straight again. It formed a very pretty picture,o The mermaids' cave, toilet 'ashore." That will be a day they will ever remember, and that we should be srgry to forget. ' Now the tiden-on nearly at its height- to the doeMr twain turnoi her head to the out and Rural away for Heylake, where we intended passing the night. A light wind from
the south gave us teufficieitt way in stem the swells, and the warmth, the 'anti:tilt, and the clear green water made it very, pleastnt Entering the lake he the !tedsttnes

ere 'dropped anchor on a place ;here we knew the cockles were to be found. Pc floe theebbing out we made ourselves snug in the twatle twttom and prenatel to make up for past deticiencies of 'deep. In this way you lay here the natives, and can select the beat. Profemionals rake for them and then riddle them free of the sated and youngsters. WINSFORD IMPROVEMENTS. Sir,—There is no doubt some rule guiding the Winsford Loml Board or its surveyor in the efforts to put this town on a similar footing with other towns round about. Anyone familiar with the nature of the place mutt be aware that tome parts must have their claime attended to sooner than others. The nature of the ground, as to whether it would require doing again in • short period, or would stand fora long time, must be one consideration. Then the frequency of its intercommunication must rule in a large degree so that some parts should bet done up many time. br,fore others are touched; and such like prudential motives as these must guide action. The summer has all but gone, with its dust and glare, but in parte the water cart has never even made its appearance saving once, or, at farthest, twice. The Caraway in some paru is yet :untouched for sloppy winter coming on, except a few loose cinders as in olden time.. True, there is a bit of paved gutter, which, as in lihth.etreet formerly, will furnish the driest walk in winter,and such rate- payersan live there moat be content with small mercies : pay the rates and nay nothing, but be thankful they can do any- thing for the good of the rest. Of course it will he their turn when nobody else wants anything doing. Lao, not aware such views are allowed to rule in other towns. From the little acquaintance I have with them, I should judge otherwise. In many towns no sooner is a street even begun, than the curb atones must he set out, the street fixed of pro- per width, and every arrangement made to meet the inhabi- tamt who commence to build there. But then these towns hare been under proper loml government for a time, and a new hotly requires training. You see, Mr. Editor, I have not been particular in pointing out any special street, for there are several to which thin description will apply, to pass along which in day light requires care for luau or bract,, on account of ruts. How much more so in the dark, especially now, wheu we have no gas lights in the street, lloping my few remarks will meet the eyes of three CIII• cerned,—l eel, yen., OBSERVER. Winsford, September Ist, 1880.

The Bret meeting to consider the desirability of celebrating I the Sunday action' centenary in the town of Widn. was held on the let July, when en Executive Committee, eon- sisting of Messrs. Thom. limy, William Jackson, Charles Brown. Benjamin Brown, 1 horn. Sadler. end Samuel Owens (tecretarv), were appointed. Arrangements were made with the litailniay Company to keep open the level mossings on the day of the centenary celebratioe, and with the police to guard the line at route. Various other meetings were after- wards held. The 24th of July was at brat fixol upon as the day on which to hold the cehbration, but as some dissatis- faction was eta-pressed at this, a general meeting was held. st which it was agreed that it should tale place on the 29th ult. It was resolved that the schoels should walk in the order of seniority, and the children should milect sulrecrip-; Gone for the expenses. About 3,000 medals were ordered front the Sunday School Union. A communication was re- ceived from the Welsh Calvinistic Methalists Mating that, owing to certaiu circumstancee, they had decided not to join in thedemonstration. The offer of the Star of Temperance /tram Band to place their eervices at the diaposal of the committee for the day waa accepted. div.head: MR. GLADSIONE'S SEA TRIP.
div.p: MR. GLADSIONE'S SEA TRIP.

' The Grantully Castle, with Mr. Oladdone on board, arrived in the Clyde early on Monday morning. A nember of gentlemen representing the public bodies of Gre..nock waited upon the Premier during the forenoon to congratulate hint on the improvement in his health. In replying Mr. (iladetone said , I assure yen, gentlemen, the value of your . demonstration in the more important in proportion as it in informal and spontaneoun. It proves to me that it is the result el your own natural feeliog. It is not so vary long since I was in Scotland for some time, in a Mite of con- miderable activity, which I cannot now pretend. (Laughter.) I have not forgotten that period, nor shall! permit myself !to do so. Still lees have I forgotten the attitude of the • people of Scotland, and the remarkable indications they gave of their view, on the situation of public affairs, or ' the immense effect that moral and political demonstration produced throughout the country. (Applause.) All these are subjectn which are cherished in your memories as lIILICh WI they are in mine. I beg to thank you for the caution you have given me not to work to hard as I have been doing for some time peat. At the age to which I have attained lam not quite fit for the same amount of work as in my better days, but I ern nurrounded by colleagues in whom I have every confidence, and who, you know, are • great deal more than worthy of their positions, and I can say they are fit for the task to which they have addressed themselves. In this, the first session of our new Parliament, we have not been unmindful of ir unfaithful to the declarations made at the time of tha elections, and it in now for nie to give you the ...nee that ar we have begun en will we continue. (Applause.) As we have begun no we will end, let that be Alen it may. A very impressive religion, service wae held on board the Grantully Castle, on Sunday night, in the main saloon. The Union Jack was spread for an altar cloth. The Rev. S. Gladetene, son of the Premier, officiated, and the Prime Minister read the lesson. All the officers anch crew who could be spared from duty were prenent. During Monday nighereels and Highland dances were kept up on the deck. and Highland mous were sung. The Premier himself joined in the procenaion which followed the piper round the ship, arm-in-ann. On the resuniption of the voyage on Wednesday, the ration. •pots of Instorical in- termt were pointed out to Mr. Gladstone as they came in night, and about thirty of the party, including the Prime Minister, landed in Scavaig Loch, Skye, and remained on shore about two hours. Mr. Gladstone went as far and as f.t up and down the steep mountain paths as any of the party. Mr. Gladstone wan rowed back to the ship by the aailom, and his son rowed in one of the other boats The Prime Minister impired his crow by leading in "Raw, brothers, row," and he also sang snatches of Venetian boat nano, but bri arriving at the Grantully Castle he immedi- ately set to work on his despatchen. He passes his time chiefly in reading, but also interests himself in the details of the working and construction of the ship and her adaptability ti purposes of naval warfare. The Premier's recovery is said to be progressing very favourably. The Urantully Cagle anriveot on Thursday afternoon in Leith Roads and Mr. GIADSTON6 was waited upon by re- presentatives of the Edinburgh and Leith Town Councils and inembers of the local Liberal associations. In replying to their congratulations on his recovery, the right hon, gentleman, alluding to the House of Common., said that when he retEcted on the severe hamar that House bad lately been engaged in performing, and rememlereol that he wan exempted from It, feelings almoat of involuntary nhame arose within him, which, were, however, mitigated by the thought that Iris colleagues had proved themselves, as he well knew they wool I, equal to the task put upon them. For himself and his colleagues, he desired that they might deserve the cond- i &nee of their countrymen at large by acting firmly and con- siderately on their convictions, and by giving the lie to those nuperlioial observers of public affairs who contend that there is no reality in the profe.ions of public men, and who maintain that they make certain declarations when out of office for the only parpose of getting into power.

They were led to such rm flections by the lives of three great English web, of the preeent century—Byron, who died at the age of 30, Beats when he was 25 end Shelley when he had nearly completed hie 30th year. Of the three Keats had the shortest Erne in which to develop and ilieplay Ills wonderful power.; and no one could tell ts what a height he might have at- tained in the republic of letters if he had bout tot greater age. hectic light was extinguished when it .hone at itn full blaze. Ile couldnot hope to have done better work, but his productions would have been greatly multiplied, had he lived. Shelley, however, died by an accident, and with a mind for more complex and higher, and more ambitious aims than theirs he needed & longer life to perfect hie power., and to recover himself front the warping influences of his youth. His early death was therefore the more to be re- gretted. Alter a graphic genealrgical sketch of the Shelley Incur, the speaker went on to my that Percy Bys•he Shelley was born in the purple of the equirearchy ; but gifted as he was with a metaphysical acuteness to diocese truth and falsehood, and bent as he was on piercing to the truth beneath all the ahams and fictions woven by society and custom, hie high social position, how,iver respectable in the ordinary point of view, was not the most fortunate for hie peace of ininil. His intense individuality led him into war with the world's opinion, and the circumetances of his birth and his surroundings only added I uel to the fire. He bad a sovereign contempt for the univeraal idol—money. At thirteen Shelley went to Eton. but he was not popular either with hie , teachers or elder shoolfellowe, although the hove of hie own I age adored him. Ile was rolled "the Atheist,'' a title which Hogg said was conferred from time to time by the boys upon the one who was the most daring in his defiance of authority. In 1809 [IC left Eton and returned home, where he fell deeperately in love with hie cousin, Harriet Grove. There wee every likelihood of this attachment resulting in inarri.ig,.. hut the speculative doubts on mmy serioue sub- jects which hie lettere contained alarmed the parents of the young lady for her future welfare, and, on Shelley being expelled from Oxford, the intimacy was broken off, and Mien Grove married oome one else, which was a terrible blow to Shelley. The expulsion from the university was calmed by hie writing and circulating among the authorities and members of his college a small pamphlet in which he met forth what he conceived to be the defective logic of the usual argument. in favour ef the existence of a God.
